patient.name: Grace Mensah
patient.complaint: Leaking urine when she coughs, laughs or goes to her exercise class
background: Three vaginal deliveries, one forceps delivery
Drinks six cups of coffee a day
Works as a bus controller in Lewisham

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' where the leak pattern decides the type: exertion = stress, sudden urge = urge, dribbling with a big bladder = overflow, normal bladder but cannot get there = functional.

points: Grace, 56, leaks **small amounts** when she coughs, sneezes or laughs.
Worse over two years; now wears pads to her Zumba class.
Occasional rush to the toilet after coffee, but no leak then.
No constant dribbling; stream is normal.
No back pain, numbness or leg weakness.

steps.lead: Grace has **involuntary leakage of urine**. The job now is to decide which type, knowing many women have a mixed picture.
Grace collects risk factors: **multiparity**, a forceps delivery, **menopause** and **obesity**.
Leaking **with exertion** and a normal stream already point to stress rather than overflow.

steps.q: Grace leaks small volumes on coughing and exercise with no real urgency. Which type fits best?
steps.r: Small-volume leak with a rise in **intra-abdominal pressure** and no major urgency is **stress incontinence**.

steps.lead: Grace's pattern matches the stress row: **cough, sneeze, laugh, exercise**, small volumes, weak pelvic floor after childbirth.

head: Type
Trigger / pattern

steps.lead: Grace has **no constant leak**, so a vesicovaginal fistula is unlikely despite her forceps delivery.

steps.text: **Constant** leakage day and night after a prolonged or obstructed labour is a **fistula**, not stress incontinence. Stress leaks only with exertion.

steps.lead: Grace has no back pain, saddle numbness or leg weakness. New retention with these needs **urgent** assessment for cauda equina syndrome.

steps.title: Spot the type from the history
nodes: Dribbling, poor stream, big bladder → overflow
Normal bladder, cannot get there → functional
steps.caption: The pattern of leakage points to the cause.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?': urine dipstick for stress, bladder diary for urge, bladder scan for overflow, and urodynamics only if unsure or before surgery.

steps.q: What is the most appropriate first investigation for Grace's stress symptoms?
steps.r: A **urine dipstick** first excludes UTI and diabetes (glycosuria) as causes or contributors.

steps.lead: Grace's dipstick is clear. Her occasional coffee urgency earns a **3-day bladder diary** too, to check for a mixed picture.

visual.title: Grace's 3-day bladder diary
visual.caption: Normal frequency; every leak was linked to coughing or exercise, not urgency.

steps.text: The diary shows frequency, leaks, triggers and fluid intake.

visual.title: Post-void residual volume

steps.text: A bladder scan matters most when overflow is suspected.

steps.lead: Grace needs **urodynamics** only if the type stays unclear or if surgery is being planned.

steps.text: Urodynamics is never first-line. It comes before **surgery** for stress or **botulinum toxin** for urge (to prove detrusor overactivity).

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' or 'next step': stress = pelvic floor training 3 to 4 months, then duloxetine, then surgery; urge = bladder retraining, antimuscarinic, mirabegron, then botulinum toxin.

steps.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment for Grace?
steps.r: **Supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least 3 months** is first-line for stress incontinence.

steps.lead: Grace starts **pelvic floor training for 3 to 4 months**, plus weight loss, less caffeine and treating her constipation.

points: Grace is referred to a women's health physiotherapist.
She cuts coffee to two cups and starts a weight programme.
Laxatives and fibre for her constipation.

visual.title: Leaks per week on pelvic floor training
visual.caption: Better, but still leaking at 4 months: time for second-line.

steps.lead: Still bothered at 4 months and not wanting surgery, Grace could try **duloxetine**, reviewed after 2 to 4 weeks.
If Grace's stress incontinence stays severe, she is **considered for surgery**, after urodynamics.
Overflow and functional incontinence are not treated with these ladders: fix the **cause** (alpha-blocker for BPH, catheter for retention, mobility, cognition).

steps.text: Antimuscarinics (oxybutynin) in a frail or confused older patient can worsen **dementia**, cause falls, retention and constipation. **Mirabegron** is safer.

steps.lead: Grace's plan follows **NICE NG123**: conservative measures first, drugs second, surgery after specialist assessment.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanism questions: why stress, urge and overflow leak, and how antimuscarinics (M3 block) and mirabegron (beta-3 agonist) work.

points: Grace asks: 'Why do I leak when I laugh?'
You draw her the bladder and the pelvic floor.

steps.lead: Childbirth weakened Grace's pelvic floor, so a cough pushes bladder pressure above her **urethral closure pressure**.

steps.title: Stress leak mechanism
nodes: Pressure exceeds urethral closure pressure → leak

steps.lead: Urge is different: the **detrusor contracts by itself** during filling and overrides cortical inhibition.
In overflow, the bladder is chronically full and **overdistended**, so urine dribbles out past the sphincter.

steps.q: Oxybutynin reduces urge leakage by blocking which receptor?
steps.r: Detrusor contraction is driven by acetylcholine at **M3** receptors; blocking them also causes dry mouth, constipation and confusion.

steps.lead: This is why Grace would get **duloxetine**, not oxybutynin: her detrusor is normal. Antimuscarinics and mirabegron target the detrusor in urge.
Grace's lower urinary tract has an outlet problem. In functional incontinence the tract is **intact** and the barrier is external.

steps.text: Match drug to mechanism: **M3 block** and **beta-3 agonism** relax the detrusor (urge); **duloxetine** boosts urethral sphincter tone (stress); **alpha-blockers** relax the prostate (overflow).

mcq.q: Leakage of small volumes on coughing and sneezing with no urgency is which type?
mcq.r: Exertional leak from raised intra-abdominal pressure is stress incontinence.

mcq.q: Leaking when putting the key in the front door ('latchkey') suggests which type?
mcq.r: Triggered sudden urgency is classic urge incontinence (overactive bladder).

mcq.q: Which red flags with new retention suggest cauda equina syndrome?
o: Back pain, saddle anaesthesia, leg weakness
mcq.r: New retention plus back pain, saddle anaesthesia or leg weakness needs urgent assessment.

mcq.q: Constant leakage after a prolonged labour suggests which diagnosis?
mcq.r: A fistula leaks constantly; it is investigated with urinary dye studies.

mcq.q: What is the first-line investigation for suspected urge incontinence?
o: Bladder diary for at least 3 days
mcq.r: A bladder diary for at least 3 days is first-line for urge.
A high post-void residual on bladder scan confirms chronic retention with overflow.

mcq.q: What is first-line treatment for stress incontinence?
o: Pelvic floor muscle training for 3-4 months
mcq.r: Pelvic floor muscle training for 3 to 4 months, plus lifestyle measures.

mcq.q: Which second-line drug for urge is preferred in the elderly?
mcq.r: Mirabegron avoids anticholinergic effects on cognition, falls and glaucoma.

mcq.q: What must be shown before botulinum toxin for refractory urge?
mcq.r: Botulinum toxin requires urodynamic confirmation of detrusor overactivity.
A beta-3 agonist relaxes the detrusor without anticholinergic effects.

prompts.q: Name the four types of urinary incontinence and the leak pattern of each.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem gives you the pattern of leakage; you name the type.

points.p: Stress: small leaks with cough, sneeze, laugh or exercise
points.why: No major urgency is the clue that separates it from urge.

points.p: Urge: sudden urgency then leakage, with frequency and nocturia
points.why: Triggers include running water, coffee and arriving home ('latchkey').

points.p: Overflow: dribbling from chronic retention, distended bladder
points.why: Look for BPH, poor stream, hesitancy or anticholinergic drugs.

points.p: Functional: normal bladder but cannot reach the toilet in time
points.why: The urinary tract is intact; the barrier is external.

prompts.q: What are the main risk factors for urinary incontinence?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: stems for stress feature multiparous, menopausal, obese women; overflow features older men.

points.p: Older age
points.why: Incontinence is common but never 'just normal ageing'.

points.p: Pregnancy, childbirth (multiparity) and pelvic floor weakness
points.why: Forceps or prolonged labour weakens the pelvic floor.

points.p: Menopause and obesity
points.why: Both raise the risk of stress incontinence.

points.p: Men: BPH or prostate problems
points.why: Prostate obstruction drives overflow.

points.p: Neurological disease, cognitive impairment and medications
points.why: Anticholinergics can cause retention and overflow.

prompts.q: Which bladder triggers point to urge incontinence rather than stress?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'cannot get there in time' after a trigger is urge.

points.p: Running water
points.why: Sound of running water triggers detrusor contraction.

points.p: Coffee or tea (caffeine)
points.why: Excess caffeine is a contributory factor.

points.p: Arriving home: latchkey incontinence
points.why: A classic SBA buzzword for urge.

points.p: Frequency and nocturia
points.why: Urge is part of overactive bladder syndrome.

prompts.q: Which features point to overflow incontinence, and what causes it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: an older man with poor stream and dribbling has a big bladder until proven otherwise.

points.p: Dribbling, poor stream, hesitancy, nocturia
points.why: Voiding symptoms suggest outflow obstruction.

points.p: Distended bladder and high post-void residual
points.why: A dull, palpable suprapubic mass is the bladder.

points.p: Causes: BPH, urethral obstruction, neuropathy or spinal cord disease, diabetes, Parkinson's
points.why: Diabetic neuropathy gives an atonic bladder.

points.p: Anticholinergic drugs
points.why: Starting oxybutynin in a man with BPH can precipitate retention.

prompts.q: What must you not miss in a patient with incontinence: key differential and red flags?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: constant leak = fistula; new retention plus back pain = cauda equina.

points.p: Vesicovaginal fistula: constant leakage after difficult or prolonged labour
points.why: Investigated with urinary dye studies.

points.p: Cauda equina: new retention or overflow with back pain
points.why: This needs urgent assessment and MRI.

points.p: Saddle anaesthesia or leg weakness
points.why: Any of these with retention is a surgical emergency.

prompts.q: What is the first-line investigation for each type of incontinence?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: match the test to the type in the stem.

points.p: Urge: bladder diary for at least 3 days
points.why: Records voids, leaks, triggers and fluid intake.

points.p: Stress: urine dipstick to rule out UTI and diabetes
points.why: Infection and glycosuria can cause or worsen leakage.

points.p: Overflow: bladder scan / post-void residual volume
points.why: A high residual confirms retention.

points.p: Functional: history and urine dip suffice
points.why: No bladder test is needed when the bladder is normal.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: urodynamics is never the first test.

points.p: Diagnostic uncertainty about the type
points.why: Mixed or atypical pictures need pressure studies.

points.p: Before surgery for stress incontinence
points.why: Surgery is only planned with a clear diagnosis.

points.p: Before botulinum toxin, to confirm detrusor overactivity
points.why: Toxin requires urodynamic proof of detrusor overactivity.

prompts.q: What is the treatment ladder for stress incontinence?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'initial management' is almost always pelvic floor training.

points.p: First-line: pelvic floor muscle training for 3-4 months
points.why: Supervised training for at least 3 months.

points.p: Lifestyle: weight loss, reduce caffeine, manage constipation
points.why: Offered alongside pelvic floor training.

points.p: Second-line: duloxetine (SNRI), reviewed after 2-4 weeks
points.why: For women who decline or are unfit for surgery.

points.p: Severe: surgery
points.why: After urodynamics.

prompts.q: What is the treatment ladder for urge incontinence, and the cautions?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the elderly, confused or falling patient gets mirabegron, not oxybutynin.

points.p: First-line: bladder retraining
points.why: For at least 6 weeks before or alongside drugs.

points.p: Then an antimuscarinic: oxybutynin, tolterodine, solifenacin
points.why: Side effects: dementia, falls, glaucoma, retention, constipation, confusion.

points.p: Second-line: mirabegron, preferred in elderly and myasthenia gravis
points.why: Avoids anticholinergic effects.

points.p: Third-line: botulinum toxin, after urodynamic confirmation
points.why: Refractory urge only.

prompts.q: How are overflow and functional incontinence managed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: treat the cause, not the bladder.

points.p: Overflow from BPH: alpha-blocker (e.g. tamsulosin)
points.why: Relaxes prostatic smooth muscle to relieve obstruction.

points.p: Acute retention: catheterisation
points.why: Decompresses the bladder.

points.p: Functional: address mobility or cognitive problems
points.why: Commodes, toileting schedules and treating delirium.

prompts.q: Explain the mechanism of stress, urge and overflow incontinence.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the pressure that is beaten in each.

points.p: Stress: intra-abdominal pressure exceeds urethral closure pressure
points.why: Weak pelvic floor or urethral sphincter.

points.p: Urge: involuntary detrusor contractions during filling override cortical inhibition
points.why: Detrusor overactivity.

points.p: Overflow: chronic retention overdistends the bladder until pressure exceeds sphincter resistance
points.why: From outlet obstruction or an atonic detrusor.

prompts.q: How do antimuscarinics and mirabegron relax the bladder?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the receptor is the answer to 'mechanism of action'.

points.p: Antimuscarinics block M3 receptors that mediate detrusor contraction
points.why: This also explains dry mouth, constipation and confusion.

points.p: Mirabegron is a beta-3 agonist that relaxes the detrusor
points.why: No anticholinergic side effects.

glossary.Stress incontinence: Leakage of urine when intra-abdominal pressure rises (cough, sneeze, exercise) because the pelvic floor or sphincter is weak.
glossary.Urge incontinence: Leakage after a sudden strong urge to pass urine, caused by detrusor overactivity.
glossary.Overflow incontinence: Dribbling leakage from a chronically over-full bladder due to retention.
glossary.Functional incontinence: Leakage with a normal bladder because the person cannot reach the toilet in time.
glossary.Mixed urinary incontinence: Features of both stress and urge incontinence in the same person.
glossary.Overactive bladder: Urgency with frequency and nocturia, with or without urge incontinence.
glossary.OAB: Overactive bladder: urgency, frequency and nocturia from detrusor overactivity.
glossary.Detrusor: The smooth muscle of the bladder wall that contracts to empty it.
glossary.Detrusor overactivity: Involuntary detrusor contractions during bladder filling, seen on urodynamics.
glossary.Urethral closure pressure: The pressure the urethra and pelvic floor hold against to keep urine in.
glossary.Pelvic floor: Sheet of muscles supporting the bladder, uterus and bowel and helping close the urethra.
glossary.Multiparity: Having given birth to several children.
glossary.Nocturia: Waking at night to pass urine.
glossary.Hesitancy: Delay in starting the urine stream.
glossary.Post-void residual: Volume of urine left in the bladder after passing urine, measured by bladder scan.
glossary.PVR: Post-void residual volume: urine left after voiding; a high value means retention.
glossary.Bladder diary: A record over at least 3 days of fluid intake, voids, leaks and triggers.
glossary.Urodynamics: Pressure studies of bladder filling and voiding, used when the diagnosis is unclear or before surgery.
glossary.Urodynamic studies: Bladder pressure tests that show detrusor overactivity or stress leakage.
glossary.Latchkey incontinence: Urge leakage triggered by arriving home and putting the key in the door.
glossary.Vesicovaginal fistula: An abnormal opening between bladder and vagina causing constant leakage, often after obstructed labour.
glossary.Cauda equina syndrome: Compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots causing retention, saddle anaesthesia and leg weakness; an emergency.
glossary.Saddle anaesthesia: Loss of sensation around the perineum and inner thighs, a red flag for cauda equina.
glossary.BPH: Benign prostatic hyperplasia: non-cancerous prostate enlargement causing outflow obstruction.
glossary.Antimuscarinic: Drug blocking muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, e.g. oxybutynin, to relax the detrusor.
glossary.Oxybutynin: Antimuscarinic for urge incontinence; can cause confusion, dry mouth and constipation in older people.
glossary.Mirabegron: Beta-3 agonist that relaxes the detrusor; second-line for urge, preferred in the elderly.
glossary.Duloxetine: An SNRI used second-line for stress incontinence; it increases urethral sphincter tone.
glossary.Botulinum toxin: Injected into the bladder wall for refractory urge incontinence to paralyse the detrusor.
glossary.Alpha-blocker: Drug such as tamsulosin that relaxes prostate smooth muscle to improve urine flow.
glossary.Tamsulosin: An alpha-1 blocker for BPH that eases outflow obstruction.
glossary.M3 receptor: Muscarinic receptor on the detrusor that mediates bladder contraction.
glossary.Bladder retraining: Gradually lengthening the time between voids to reduce urgency; first-line for urge.
glossary.Pelvic floor muscle training: Supervised exercises for at least 3 months; first-line for stress incontinence.
glossary.Glycosuria: Glucose in the urine, suggesting diabetes.
glossary.NICE NG123: NICE guideline on urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in women.

technique.stem: A 64 year old woman has a 6 month history of a sudden, strong need to pass urine, often leaking before she reaches the toilet. It is worse when she hears running water and when she arrives home. She passes urine 12 times a day and twice at night. She drinks five cups of tea daily. Abdominal examination is normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: It asks for the type of incontinence, so read the leak pattern.

clues: sudden, strong need to pass urine
12 times a day and twice at night
steps.x: Urgency first, then leak; classic triggers; frequency and nocturia; caffeine.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Urgency with triggers = **detrusor overactivity** = urge incontinence.

elim: Functional needs a mobility or cognitive barrier; she is well.
Mixed needs stress leaks too; none with cough or exercise.
Overflow gives dribbling and a distended bladder; abdomen normal.
Stress leaks with cough or exertion, without urgency.

steps.x: **E. Urge incontinence.** Rule: urgency + running water/latchkey + frequency = urge.

technique.stem: A 64 year old woman has sudden urgency to pass urine with occasional leakage before reaching the toilet. She also passes urine frequently and gets up twice at night. Urine dipstick is negative. She has not tried any treatment yet.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: Bladder diary for at least 3 days

steps.x: Initial investigation: the cheapest first test that guides treatment.
Urge picture, untreated, dipstick already clear.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: For urge, the first-line test is a **bladder diary for at least 3 days**.

elim: Cystoscopy is for haematuria or suspected bladder lesions.
Bladder scan is first-line for suspected overflow.
Ultrasound kidneys is not needed for uncomplicated urge.
Urodynamics only if unsure or before surgery/toxin.

steps.x: **A. Bladder diary.** Rule: urge → diary ≥3 days; stress → dip; overflow → bladder scan.

technique.stem: An 82 year old woman has urge incontinence. Six weeks of bladder retraining has not helped. She has mild cognitive impairment and has had two falls this year, one after standing up quickly. Urine dipstick is negative and her post-void residual volume is 40 mL.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

steps.x: Next step after bladder retraining fails, so pick the right drug for her.
Elderly, cognitive impairment, falls and postural symptoms: anticholinergic burden matters.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Antimuscarinics worsen cognition and falls, so choose **mirabegron** (beta-3 agonist).

elim: Botulinum toxin is third-line and needs urodynamic proof.
Duloxetine is second-line for stress, not urge.
Oxybutynin can worsen dementia, confusion and falls in the elderly.
Tamsulosin is for overflow from BPH.

steps.x: **C. Mirabegron.** Rule: frail or confused elderly with urge → mirabegron over antimuscarinic.

technique.stem: A 70 year old woman with overactive bladder is started on oxybutynin. Her urgency improves, but two weeks later she has a dry mouth, constipation and new confusion.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of action of this drug?

steps.x: Mechanism of the named drug, confirmed by its side effects.

clues: dry mouth, constipation and new confusion
steps.x: Classic anticholinergic side effects.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Oxybutynin blocks **M3** receptors that drive detrusor contraction.

elim: 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (finasteride) shrink the prostate.
Alpha-blockers relax the prostate in BPH.
Beta-3 agonism is mirabegron, with no anticholinergic effects.
SNRI action is duloxetine for stress incontinence.

steps.x: **D. M3 antagonism.** Rule: antimuscarinic = M3 block = dry, constipated, confused.

practice.stem: A 48 year old woman has a 1 year history of leaking small amounts of urine when she coughs, laughs or goes running. She has no urgency and passes urine six times a day. She has had four vaginal deliveries and her BMI is 31 kg/m². Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. Abdominal examination is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: name the type from the leak pattern.

clues: small amounts of urine when she coughs, laughs or goes running
steps.x: Exertional small leaks, multiparous, obese, no urgency.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Raised intra-abdominal pressure beats a weak pelvic floor: **stress incontinence**.

elim: Functional needs a mobility or cognitive barrier.
Overflow gives dribbling and a distended bladder.
Urge has sudden urgency first; she has none.
UTI gives dysuria and frequency, not 1 year of exertional leaks.

steps.x: **C. Stress incontinence.** Rule: cough/laugh/exercise + multiparity = stress.

practice.e: Small leaks with cough, laugh or exercise and no urgency in a multiparous woman is stress incontinence. Urge would start with a sudden need to void.

practice.stem: A 69 year old woman has a 4 month history of a sudden urge to pass urine, leaking before she reaches the toilet. It happens most when she puts her key in the front door. She gets up three times at night. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 142/84 mmHg. Abdominal and vaginal examinations are normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: type of incontinence.

clues: puts her key in the front door
steps.x: Urgency then leak, latchkey trigger, nocturia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Latchkey trigger = **urge incontinence** (detrusor overactivity).

elim: She is mobile and cognitively well, so not functional.
No dribbling or palpable bladder, so not overflow.
Stress leaks with exertion, not after urgency.
Afebrile and 4 months long; UTI is acute with dysuria.

steps.x: **D. Urge incontinence.** Rule: latchkey or running water = urge.

practice.e: Leaking after a sudden urge, triggered by arriving home, with nocturia is urge incontinence from detrusor overactivity. Stress leaks only on exertion.

practice.stem: A 78 year old man has a 6 month history of constant dribbling of urine, a poor stream and hesitancy. He has to get up four times at night. A smooth, dull swelling is palpable above the pubis that does not go away after he passes urine.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: type, and the examination finding is the key.

clues: dull swelling is palpable above the pubis
does not go away after he passes urine
steps.x: Voiding symptoms plus a bladder that stays full.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Chronic retention (likely BPH) with dribbling = **overflow incontinence**.

elim: Functional means a normal bladder; his is distended.
Stress leaks on exertion and the bladder empties.
Urge gives urgency, not a palpable bladder.
UTI does not cause a painless persistent distended bladder.

steps.x: **B. Overflow incontinence.** Rule: dribbling + palpable bladder after voiding = overflow.

practice.e: A palpable bladder after voiding with dribbling, poor stream and hesitancy is chronic retention with overflow, usually from BPH. Urge incontinence has an empty bladder.

practice.stem: An 86 year old woman with Alzheimer's dementia is admitted after a hip fracture repair. She is incontinent of urine several times a day, usually while trying to find the toilet. Before admission she was continent. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm, BP 132/76 mmHg and temperature 36.8°C. Her post-void residual volume is 30 mL.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: which type in a frail inpatient.

clues: while trying to find the toilet
steps.x: Cognitive and mobility barrier; bladder empties normally; urine clear.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Normal bladder, cannot get there in time = **functional incontinence**.

elim: Overflow needs a high residual; hers is 30 mL.
No exertional leak pattern.
No urgency described; the barrier is finding the toilet.
Dipstick negative and afebrile.

steps.x: **A. Functional incontinence.** Rule: dementia or immobility + normal bladder = functional.

practice.e: With a normal post-void residual and clear urine, her leakage comes from dementia and immobility: functional incontinence. Overflow would show a large residual.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man has 2 days of severe low back pain after lifting. Today he noticed dribbling of urine and numbness around his anus and inner thighs. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 146/88 mmHg. Both ankle reflexes are reduced. A bladder scan shows 900 mL of urine.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: the cause of new overflow with neurology.

clues: severe low back pain after lifting
numbness around his anus and inner thighs
steps.x: New painless retention with overflow, back pain and saddle anaesthesia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: This is the red flag complication: **cauda equina syndrome**, needing urgent MRI.

elim: BPH is slow and has no back pain or saddle numbness.
Diabetic neuropathy is gradual, with no acute back pain.
MS is unlikely with acute lifting injury and saddle loss.
UTI does not cause saddle anaesthesia or reduced reflexes.

steps.x: **B. Cauda equina syndrome.** Rule: new retention + back pain + saddle anaesthesia = emergency MRI.

practice.e: New retention with overflow, back pain and saddle anaesthesia is cauda equina syndrome until proven otherwise. BPH causes slow, painless obstruction.

practice.stem: A 76 year old man has a 1 year history of a weak stream, hesitancy and terminal dribbling, with leakage of small amounts of urine through the day. He was started on oxybutynin 3 weeks ago for urgency and the leakage has become worse. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?

steps.x: Examination finding, so predict the type first.

clues: weak stream, hesitancy and terminal dribbling
steps.x: Outflow obstruction, then an anticholinergic: retention with overflow.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Overflow incontinence: expect a **distended, dull, painless bladder**.

elim: Ankle reflexes are for peripheral neuropathy or cord lesions, not BPH.
Lax anal tone suggests cauda equina; no back pain here.
Saddle anaesthesia is also a cauda equina sign.
Renal angle tenderness means pyelonephritis.

steps.x: **C. Painless dull suprapubic mass.** Rule: BPH + antimuscarinic = retention with overflow.

practice.e: Oxybutynin in a man with BPH can cause chronic retention with overflow, giving a palpable, dull, painless bladder. Cauda equina signs need back pain and neurology.

practice.stem: A 54 year old woman has leaked urine on coughing and sneezing for 9 months. She has no urgency or dysuria. She has had three vaginal deliveries. Her pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. Abdominal examination is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: Bladder diary for at least 3 days

steps.x: Initial investigation for this type.
Typical stress incontinence.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: First-line for stress: **urine dipstick** to exclude UTI and diabetes.

elim: Bladder diary is first-line for urge.
Cystoscopy is not part of routine assessment.
Bladder scan is first-line when overflow is suspected.
Urodynamics only if uncertain or surgery planned.

steps.x: **D. Urine dipstick.** Rule: stress → dip first.

practice.e: For stress incontinence the first test is a urine dipstick to rule out UTI and glycosuria. Urodynamics is reserved for uncertainty or before surgery.

practice.stem: A 59 year old woman has stress incontinence. She completed 4 months of supervised pelvic floor muscle training and tried duloxetine, without benefit. She still leaks with coughing and urgency is sometimes present. She now wants to discuss surgery.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation before surgery?
o: Bladder diary for at least 3 days

steps.x: Investigation before surgery.
Failed conservative and drug treatment; possible mixed picture; surgery planned.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Surgery planned + uncertainty = **urodynamic studies**.

elim: A diary helps first-line, but cannot confirm the type before surgery.
CT urogram is for haematuria.
MRI pelvis is not needed for incontinence.
Dipstick is the first test, already passed.

steps.x: **E. Urodynamic studies.** Rule: surgery planned or type unclear → urodynamics.

practice.e: Urodynamics is indicated before surgery for stress incontinence and when the picture is mixed. A bladder diary is a first-line test, not a pre-operative one.

practice.stem: A 42 year old woman has leaked small amounts of urine on exercise and coughing for 6 months. She has two children. Her BMI is 29 kg/m². Urine dipstick is negative. She has had no treatment yet.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: Initial management for this type.
Untreated stress incontinence.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: First-line: **pelvic floor muscle training for 3 to 4 months** plus lifestyle advice.

elim: Duloxetine is second-line after pelvic floor training.
Surgery is for severe or refractory cases.
Mirabegron is for urge.
Oxybutynin is for urge.

steps.x: **E. Pelvic floor muscle training.** Rule: stress → PFMT 3-4 months first.

practice.e: Supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least 3 months is first-line for stress incontinence. Duloxetine is second-line and antimuscarinics treat urge.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man has a poor stream, hesitancy and dribbling incontinence. His prostate feels smooth and moderately enlarged on rectal examination. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 136/80 mmHg. He is not in pain.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: Initial management: treat the cause of this type.
BPH with chronic retention and overflow; renal function normal; no pain.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Overflow from BPH: treat the cause with an **alpha-blocker**.

elim: Duloxetine treats stress incontinence.
Mirabegron treats urge.
Oxybutynin would worsen retention.
Pelvic floor training is for stress.

steps.x: **E. Tamsulosin.** Rule: overflow from BPH → alpha-blocker.

practice.e: Overflow incontinence is treated by fixing the cause; for BPH that is an alpha-blocker such as tamsulosin. Antimuscarinics worsen retention.

practice.stem: A 66 year old woman has urge incontinence. Bladder retraining, solifenacin and then mirabegron have not helped. Urodynamic studies confirm detrusor overactivity. She is keen for further treatment.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

steps.x: Next step after first- and second-line urge treatment.

clues: Bladder retraining, solifenacin and then mirabegron
steps.x: Refractory urge, now proven on urodynamics.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Third-line for refractory urge: **botulinum toxin injection**.

elim: Duloxetine is for stress.
A sling treats stress, not detrusor overactivity.
Another antimuscarinic after failure adds little.
Tamsulosin is for BPH and overflow.

steps.x: **A. Botulinum toxin.** Rule: refractory urge + proven detrusor overactivity → botulinum toxin.

practice.e: Refractory urge incontinence with urodynamically proven detrusor overactivity is treated with bladder botulinum toxin. A sling treats stress incontinence.

practice.stem: A 51 year old woman leaks urine when she sneezes or lifts heavy boxes at work. She had a prolonged second stage of labour with her third child. Urodynamic studies show leakage during coughing without any detrusor contraction.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her leakage?
o: Intra-abdominal pressure exceeding urethral closure pressure

steps.x: Mechanism: what pressure is beaten?
Exertional leak, pelvic floor injury, no detrusor activity.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Stress incontinence: **intra-abdominal pressure exceeds urethral closure pressure**.

elim: Overdistension is overflow; no retention here.
A fistula leaks constantly, not only on exertion.
Mobility barriers cause functional incontinence.
Urodynamics showed no detrusor contraction, so not urge.

steps.x: **D.** Rule: stress = abdominal pressure beats a weak urethral closure.

practice.e: In stress incontinence a weak pelvic floor and sphincter mean a rise in intra-abdominal pressure exceeds urethral closure pressure. Detrusor contractions cause urge.
